title.heading: Rover Engineer
title.subtitle: REL — Rover Exploration Laboratory
title.coverCaption: De Gerlache crater rim, lunar south pole. The Sun skims the horizon; Earth hangs low in the north.

speedInfo: The mission compresses 14 days of lunar daylight into 5 minutes. Driving is compressed too: rovers in this game drive {compression} times faster than the real speeds their parts are modeled on.

On Apollo 15 in 1971, the crew reported that about 6 to 7 km/h was the most comfortable driving speed for the Lunar Roving Vehicle. Its top speed was of the order of 9 to 13 km/h, depending on slope, roughness, and soil.
Robotic rovers drive far slower. NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars have a top speed of about 4 cm/s (0.15 km/h) on flat ground.
design.speedInfoBuild: This build: {game} m/s in the mission, modeled on {real} km/h of real driving.
design.speedInfoSources: Sources: NASA TR R-401, Mobility Performance of the Lunar Roving Vehicle (1972); NASA/JPL Mars Science Laboratory and Mars 2020 press kits.

landing.heading: Landing
landing.briefing: The lander has touched down on the de Gerlache crater rim. The rover is deploying.

survey.heading: Orbital survey leads
survey.intro: Orbital data show three areas of interest near the landing site. Directions and distances are measured from the lander and are approximate: orbital maps locate areas, not exact sites. The rover's own survey locates each site; until then, an arrow at the edge of the map points toward each area.

layers.name: Layered wall exposure
layers.source: LOLA topography shows the steep inner wall of de Gerlache crater, where crater walls often expose old rock layers.

boulders.name: Boulder field
boulders.source: LROC images show a small fresh crater; fresh craters are ringed by boulders and soft ground.

shadow.name: Permanent shadow
shadow.source: LOLA illumination maps show a crater floor that never receives direct sunlight. Cold traps like this may hold water ice.

history.survived: India's Pragyan rover did likewise in 2023: it completed its planned one lunar day of operations, about 14 Earth days, before ISRO put it into sleep mode for the lunar night.
history.energy: NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover ended the same way: a Mars-wide dust storm covered its site, its last signal arrived on June 10, 2018, and NASA declared the mission over on February 13, 2019.
history.stuck: NASA's Spirit rover met this fate on Mars: it became stuck in soft soil on May 1, 2009, and in January 2010 NASA redefined its mission as a stationary science platform.
history.froze: India's Vikram lander and Pragyan rover entered sleep mode before the cold lunar night in September 2023, and ISRO has not reported regaining contact after its wake-up attempts around September 22.
history.destroyed: The Soviet Lunokhod 2 rover was also lost to damage: its lid touched a crater wall on May 9, 1973, dust fell onto its radiator, it overheated, and the mission was closed on June 4, 1973.
history.rollover: No planetary rover is known to have been lost to a rollover. NASA's Spirit rover had a static tip-over angle of 45 degrees, and its software stopped a drive whenever its tilt passed a set limit.

marsSoon.heading: Mars: coming soon
marsSoon.body: The Moon campaign is complete. Research points carry forward to Mars technology.

drill.searchHintHydrogen: Inside permanent shadow. Stop and press F to test-drill. Each sample reports the hydrogen signal: the stronger it is, the closer the ice.
drill.hydrogenHistory: Orbiters search for polar ice the same way: LEND, the Russian-built neutron detector on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, maps hydrogen near the poles, because hydrogen in the soil cuts the number of neutrons escaping the surface.
drill.hydrogenSource: NASA Goddard, LRO instruments: LEND (lunar.gsfc.nasa.gov/lend.html); Mitrofanov et al. 2010, Science 330:483

tutorial.label: Tutorial
tutorial.reopen: The Help button reopens this tutorial at any time.

design.title: Parts, mass and cost
body: Select one part for each of the seven slots. Every slot starts empty, and the rover can launch only when each slot has a part; "No lights" and "No heater" count as choices. Each part has a cost, a mass and a size. The specification sheet shows the totals for the rover.
Cheap parts are heavy and light parts are expensive. A heavier rover is slower, uses more energy per meter and sinks deeper in soft ground.

design.title: Launch ticket
body: REL buys the rover a spot on the next launch. The ticket tier is the smallest one that fits both the rover's mass and its size: {tiers}.
A rover just over a tier limit pays the much higher price of the next tier. A rover above the {top} limits cannot launch. The marks on the mass and size gauges show each limit.

design.title: Chassis and budget
body: Each chassis has a maximum load. If the total mass exceeds it, the frame takes damage throughout the mission.
The parts and the ticket are paid from the budget. After the mission, the balance must meet the minimum budget for the next mission ({nextMinimum}), or the round is restarted.
Optional: the i button beside the maximum speed compares game speeds with real rover speeds.

drive.title: Driving and time
body: W A S D or arrow keys to drive. Space to brake.
The mission lasts {minutes} minutes, which represent {days} days of lunar daylight. There is no clock: time is read from the Sun, which circles low on the horizon, and from the moving shadows.

drive.title: Energy
body: The energy bar is the battery. The solar panel charges it only in sunlight; the readout under the meters shows "{sunlit}" or "{shadow}".
Driving uses more energy than the panel earns. Stop in sunlight to recharge. At zero energy the mission ends.

drive.title: Damage and cold
body: Hard impacts and ground steeper than {maxSlope}° damage the rover. A rollover ends the mission at once.
Inside permanent shadow the cold meter rises, and the rover freezes when it is full. Lights are required to enter permanent shadow; a heater slows freezing.

drive.title: Solar flares
body: When a solar flare is detected, a warning bar appears {warningSeconds} seconds before it strikes.
Before the bar runs out, power down with P or move into shadow. A powered-down rover cannot drive, but its panel still charges.

drive.title: Instrument and map

instrument.camera: Camera: C takes a photograph. Photographs count toward milestones at viewpoints, or with Earth above the horizon in view at least {earthMinDistance} m from the lander.
instrument.drill: Drill: stop the rover, then press F to drill a regolith sample. Samples count at up to three sites, each at least {sampleSpacing} m from the lander and from each other.

body: The map starts zoomed in on the lander and widens as the rover explores. It shows only ground within {revealRadius} m of where the rover has been, and sites appear once the rover finds them. Arrows at the edge of the map point toward the orbital survey leads from the landing briefing.
